{"id": "23:14/q09", "question": "How are the two bone nouns read?", "turns_on": "The transmitted forms, whether singular is generic, and the value of the plural in a body with many bones.", "positions": [{"id": "23:14/q09/p1", "position": "Both are plural: ʿiẓāman and al-ʿiẓām.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī prefers the agreement of the authoritative readers; Abū ʿAlī prefers the plural because other Qurʾānic references to bones are plural (17:49, 79:11, 36:78). A human has many bones; al-Ālūsī says shapes and hardness vary, with one reported count of 248. The rasm can hold forms with or without alif. Ibn Mujāhid explicitly assigns the plural forms to the readers other than Ibn ʿĀmir and Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim."}, {"id": "23:14/q09/p2", "position": "Both are singular: ʿaẓman and al-ʿaẓm, a generic or collective noun.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀmir and Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim are regularly named; Ḥafṣ and other transmitters differ. Al-Fārisī cites nouns such as insān and dirham and Abū Zayd's collective qarād; al-Zajjāj cites singular bone for many throats; al-Samīn cites 19:4, 2:7 and poetry about hides. It also matches singular flesh. Al-Ālūsī disputes restricting this to poetic necessity. Ibn Mujāhid specifies that Ibn ʿĀmir and Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim read both nouns in the singular, without the alif before mīm."}, {"id": "23:14/q09/p3", "position": "The first noun is singular and the second plural.", "reasons": "Ibn Jinnī prefers the progression from preceding singular embryonic nouns to general plurality; he cites poetry including Ṭufayl's singular ʿaẓm. Reports vary over the readers assigned. The singular can mean the generic substance."}, {"id": "23:14/q09/p4", "position": "The first noun is plural and the second singular.", "reasons": "Ibn Jinnī finds reverting to singular less apt than progressing from singular to plural; the singular still denotes bone collectively. Reports differ over Mujāhid's reading."}, {"id": "23:14/q09/p5", "position": "Ibn Masʿūd's wording adds sinew to bone before the flesh covering.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya report a reading in which the drop is made bone and sinew, then clothed with flesh."}]}
{"id": "23:14/q10", "question": "What bones or bodily structure are meant?", "turns_on": "Whether the singular bone denotes the skeletal substance generally or a particular axial bone.", "positions": [{"id": "23:14/q10/p1", "position": "The developing skeleton and bodily support.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr says the morsel is shaped into head, limbs, bone, sinews and veins; al-Biqāʿī describes bones from head to feet; Elmalılı calls bones the framework and pillars; al-Ālūsī stresses their variety."}, {"id": "23:14/q10/p2", "position": "The bone refers specifically to the backbone.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr reports Ibn ʿAbbās's identification and a Ṣaḥīḥ hadith that all of Adam's body decays except the tailbone, from which he was created and will be reassembled."}]}
{"id": "23:14/q11", "question": "What is meant by clothing bones with flesh?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:14/q11/p1", "position": "God grows or places flesh around bones, covering, binding, and strengthening them like clothing.", "reasons": "Al-Dāmghānī includes sinews, veins, flesh and skin (2:259); Ibn Kathīr, al-Biqāʿī, Bursevī and Elmalılı mention fitted cover and support. Al-Bayḍāwī says the flesh is leftover morsel or nourishment grown onto bone; al-Ālūsī says leftover flesh or new flesh from womb blood. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the wording need not imply an interval of bare bone."}, {"id": "23:14/q11/p2", "position": "The clothing expression is a metaphor for flesh covering bone.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says flesh is pictured as clothing; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls it a subtle implied metaphor."}]}
{"id": "23:14/q12", "question": "To whom does the pronoun in anshaʾnāhu refer?", "turns_on": "Whether the antecedent is the person already named or the developing physical entity.", "positions": [{"id": "23:14/q12/p1", "position": "It refers to the human being under formation.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī connects it with the human of 15:26; al-Farrāʾ names the human; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says it refers to the person whose bones were clothed, distinct in essence and properties from the material body."}, {"id": "23:14/q12/p2", "position": "It refers to the bone, drop and lump conceived as one entity, or the thing just mentioned.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī and al-Farrāʾ allow a unified entity of the prior materials; al-Nasafī says it can refer to the immediately mentioned thing."}]}
{"id": "23:14/q13", "question": "What does anshaʾa mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the verb simply describes origination or signals a new mode of being.", "positions": [{"id": "23:14/q13/p1", "position": "To bring into being, originate, and nurture a new kind of being.", "reasons": "Al-Dāmghānī cites 21:11, 56:35, 67:23, 6:133 and 56:61; al-Rāghib, reported by al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī, joins originating and nurturing. Al-Biqāʿī reports al-Rāzī that the root letters indicate elevation or loftiness."}, {"id": "23:14/q13/p2", "position": "The shift from khalq to inshāʾ marks the emergence of a new self unlike the prior matter.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says life, knowledge and power were not contained in the earlier physical stages; the pronoun still links the person to that matter."}]}
{"id": "23:14/q14", "question": "How is the new-creation clause read?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:14/q14/p1", "position": "Ibn Masʿūd's reading adds 'for him' to the new-creation clause.", "reasons": "ʿAbd al-Razzāq attributes this wording to Ibn Masʿūd."}]}
{"id": "23:14/q15", "question": "What is the other creation?", "turns_on": "The phrase may name an event in the womb, birth, later bodily and mental development, or the entire human transformation; some commentators explicitly broaden or reconcile the readings.", "positions": [{"id": "23:14/q15/p1", "position": "The spirit is breathed into the formed fetus, making inert matter a living human.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī prefers this by analogy with Adam's clay and spirit; Ṣāḥib al-Naẓm appeals to the shift in wording. ʿAlī says an angel breathes after four months in three darknesses. Ibn Kathīr says movement, hearing, sight and perception follow and treats later life stages as compatible consequences. Al-Ālūsī notes a rational soul created for or in the body; al-Qāshānī reads God's spirit and divine image inwardly. Many early authorities are named across sources."}, {"id": "23:14/q15/p2", "position": "It is the growth of hair, or hair and teeth.", "reasons": "Qatāda is reported for hair alone and elsewhere hair plus teeth; al-Ḍaḥḥāk answers an objection about newborn hair by pointing to pubic and armpit hair. Al-Ālūsī derides that answer."}, {"id": "23:14/q15/p3", "position": "It is attainment of full youth or mature adulthood.", "reasons": "Mujāhid, Ibn ʿUmar and others are reported; Study Quran adds full realization of faculties."}, {"id": "23:14/q15/p4", "position": "It encompasses the person's successive stages after birth, from nursing through maturity and old age.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās lists crying, finding the breast, sitting, crawling, walking, weaning, eating, puberty and travel; al-Ḍaḥḥāk adds hair and age. Al-Rāzī invokes the following death verse (23:15), and Ibn Kathīr says the reading follows from ensoulment. Reports differ in exactly which stages they list."}, {"id": "23:14/q15/p5", "position": "It is the completed human form, face, spirit and faculties together.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī reports the face; al-Bayḍāwī allows form, spirit and faculties singly or all together. Al-Rāzī, al-Nasafī, al-Zamakhsharī and al-Ālūsī describe a living, speaking, hearing, seeing being, unlike inert matter. Elmalılı relates the completed form to 95:4; Taʾwīlāt al-Najmiyya stresses honor and preparedness."}, {"id": "23:14/q15/p6", "position": "It is the distinction of male and female.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan and other unnamed interpreters are reported; this locates the new creation within the womb."}, {"id": "23:14/q15/p7", "position": "It is the acquisition of reason, understanding, sensory faculties, or capacities.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī proposes discernment; al-Qushayrī lists hearing, sight, reason, perception and inspired gifts, while al-Ālūsī reports sensory faculties. Kur'an Yolu sees independent psychological and spiritual personality."}, {"id": "23:14/q15/p8", "position": "It is emergence from the womb into the world, becoming a separate creature.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās is reported for birth; Asad calls the newborn independent of its mother's body."}, {"id": "23:14/q15/p9", "position": "The phrase broadly includes speech, perception, skill, reason and all human development, beginning at ensoulment.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Qurṭubī reject confining it to one stage; Ibn Kathīr reconciles ensoulment and later stages. Ibn ʿAbbās is also reported to specify conduct in worldly affairs. Al-Qushayrī adds rare mature spiritual states of servanthood and effacement."}, {"id": "23:14/q15/p10", "position": "It is especially the inward emergence of a human formed in God's image or prepared for spiritual realization.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says the human is created yet more than merely a creature; al-Qushayrī describes release from bondage and realization of divine attributes through effacement; Taʾwīlāt al-Najmiyya calls the person repository of gnosis and divine love."}]}
{"id": "23:14/q16", "question": "Why is this called another creation?", "turns_on": "Whether otherness denotes life and faculties, bodily differentiation, or a self distinct from its material body.", "positions": [{"id": "23:14/q16/p1", "position": "Life and faculties make the human radically distinct from the inert preceding matter.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says mute matter becomes living and articulate; al-Nasafī adds hearing and sight. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī argues the knowing capable person differs essentially from the body and uses 32:10–11, where the person is taken at

Ibn ʿĀshūr says thumma marks rank; Islahi sees resurrection power in this transformation."}, {"id": "23:14/q16/p2", "position": "The human has unusually rich and differentiated bodily and personal traits.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī contrasts uniform drop with diverse flesh, bones, hair, nails, nerves, skin, brain and veins, and lists divergent temperaments and traits; al-Ālūsī reports the microcosm verse."}, {"id": "23:14/q16/p3", "position": "The person is a self that uses the body as an instrument.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī likens person and body to writer and pen and reads 32:10–11 as distinguishing them."}]}
{"id": "23:14/q17", "question": "What does the verse imply about the timing or nature of the spirit?", "turns_on": "Whether the human named by the verse is bodily composite or a distinct immaterial self, and when spirit comes to be.", "positions": [{"id": "23:14/q17/p1", "position": "The human is a composite bodily being, against a spirit-only or indivisible account.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī, al-Rāzī and Abū Ḥayyān say the described stages refute al-Naẓẓām and the philosophers or Maʿmar; al-Ālūsī reports the Imam's argument. The philosophers identify the person with an immaterial rational soul, neither divisible nor inside or outside the body."}, {"id": "23:14/q17/p2", "position": "The spirit is created after bodily formation and joins or permeates it.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says temporal thumma supports a later rational soul, the view of most Islamic theologians and Aristotle; for animal spirit this is plain. He reports disagreement whether the rational spirit attaches to or permeates the body; most Muslims say permeates."}, {"id": "23:14/q17/p3", "position": "The person is distinct in essence from the prior matter and uses the body as a tool.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī links this to being taken at death in 32:10–11 while the body disperses."}]}
{"id": "23:14/q18", "question": "Does the new-creation wording affect compensation for a usurped egg that hatches?", "turns_on": "Whether a new physical identity ends the owner's claim to the transformed property.", "positions": [{"id": "23:14/q18/p1", "position": "The taker owes the egg, not the chick, because the chick is another creation.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥanīfa's inference is transmitted by al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, Bursevī and al-Ālūsī."}, {"id": "23:14/q18/p2", "position": "The chick remains compensable as part of the owner's usurped property.", "reasons": "Al-Kashf says distinct creation does not defeat the owner's title under opponents' principles; al-Taqrīb says liability rests on its being part of the property, not on identity of names."}]}
{"id": "23:14/q19", "question": "What does tabāraka mean?", "turns_on": "Whether emphasis falls on exaltation, abundance of blessing, the root's permanence, or the verbal form.", "positions": [{"id": "23:14/q19/p1", "position": "God is exalted, holy and worthy of enduring praise.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā compares 23:116; al-Thaʿlabī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī and Ibn al-Jawzī stress God's permanence; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls it a derived form of bāraka. Al-Rāzī links blessing's increase to rising above others; al-Biqāʿī says God is fixed in perfection and free of defect. Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī add holiness and divine knowledge and power."}, {"id": "23:14/q19/p2", "position": "The word derives from firmness, settling or permanence.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī, al-Ṭabrisī and Jishumī derive it from abiding; al-Rāghib compares water settled in a pool. Ibn ʿĀshūr cites al-Raḍī that the tāfaʿala form intensifies an established state."}, {"id": "23:14/q19/p3", "position": "God possesses abundant, lasting good and pours blessing on creation.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī relays al-Rāghib's pool image for settled divine good (7:96) and connects blessing with God's measuring and creation; Ibn ʿĀshūr speaks of immense welfare decreed for people and baraka as increase. Al-Rāzī offers all blessings coming from God."}, {"id": "23:14/q19/p4", "position": "It is a past verb with a fixed, noninflecting form.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī describe its verbal form; al-Ālūsī notes it usually has a nonfeminine subject."}]}
{"id": "23:14/q20", "question": "Why does the praise follow the creation account, and why name Allah?", "turns_on": "The sources give the transition grounds in divine power and beneficence, human honor, humans' inability to praise during formation, and the majestic name.", "positions": [{"id": "23:14/q20/p1", "position": "The extraordinary formation displays God's power, wisdom and generosity and calls forth praise.", "reasons": "Al-Khaṭṭābī mentions subtle wisdom and mercy; al-Māwardī and Ibn Kathīr note favor, precise formation and resurrection power; al-Bayḍāwī, Ibn ʿĀshūr, Islahi and Kur'an Yolu connect praise with wondrous power and gratitude. Al-Ālūsī says fa introduces a concluding interjection; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī makes the closing praise universal by omitted complements."}, {"id": "23:14/q20/p2", "position": "The praise marks humanity's special honor among created beings.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī notes that God does not praise Himself this way after enumerating heavens, Throne and other beings; he links 95:4 but says divine self-praise outranks praise of humanity. Taʾwīlāt al-Najmiyya and Mathnawī verses cite 17:70 and 95:4; Kur'an Yolu says the closing praise reflects high regard for humans."}, {"id": "23:14/q20/p3", "position": "God praises Himself on behalf of humans who could not yet praise Him.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī and people of spiritual insight reported by Bursevī say humans were not able to thank Him as their stages were being described."}, {"id": "23:14/q20/p4", "position": "The majestic name Allah gathers divine names and makes the audience feel awe.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says it gathers all beautiful names; al-Ālūsī says the shift to it marks these acts as divine prerogatives and invites glorification."}]}
{"id": "23:14/q21", "question": "How is aḥsan al-khāliqīn parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether a definite annexed superlative can qualify Allah, and how an elided comparison is supplied.", "positions": [{"id": "23:14/q21/p1", "position": "Its comparative measure, 'in creating or estimating,' is elided.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī, al-Bayḍāwī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn and Bursevī say khāliqīn makes the omission understood; al-Samīn compares 22:39. Al-Ālūsī likens it to the Prophetic saying that God is beautiful, with the act understood as beautiful."}, {"id": "23:14/q21/p2", "position": "It is apposition to Allah.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafī allows apposition; Abū al-Baqāʾ denies an adjective because a comparative remains indefinite despite annexation; Bursevī adopts apposition. Al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī regard the apposition as possible but less preferred."}, {"id": "23:14/q21/p3", "position": "It is predicate of an omitted huwa.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn and Abū al-Baqāʾ list this parse; al-Samīn calls the ellipsis less likely."}, {"id": "23:14/q21/p4", "position": "Aḥsanu is an adjective of Allah.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn prefers it because derived apposition is uncommon and argues the superlative annexation can be genuinely definite; al-Ālūsī prefers the same. Jishumī calls the phrase descriptive."}]}
{"id": "23:14/q22", "question": "What does khāliqīn mean and can beings besides God be called creators?", "turns_on": "Whether khāliq describes craft, Jesus's permitted shaping, independent origination, or an intensifying superlative.", "positions": [{"id": "23:14/q22/p1", "position": "It means makers, shapers or estimators; humans can be called creators in this limited Arabic sense.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash and al-Ṭabarī cite craft usage and Zuhayr's line about finishing an object; al-Wāḥidī explains measuring leather for flasks, skins or shoes; al-Aʿlam elaborates leatherwork. Al-Layth gives feminine khāliqāt for women makers. Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Qurṭubī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī and Kur'an Yolu distinguish manufacture from origination. Al-Ṭabrisī says exact true creation belongs to God (7:54); God creates without tools or limit according to Jishumī."}, {"id": "23:14/q22/p2", "position": "The plural includes Jesus, who was allowed to create or shape.", "reasons": "Ibn Jurayj invokes Jesus and 3:49; al-Ṭabrisī distinguishes shaping clay from divine creation, and al-Burhān reports al-Qāḍī Abū Bakr's appeal to that sense. Al-Rāzī objects that the plural is broader than Jesus alone."}, {"id": "23:14/q22/p3", "position": "Only God is properly a creator; others are called this only by qualification, belief or figurative extension.", "reasons": "Some reported by al-Qurṭubī deny the name to humans; al-Kaʿbī allows it only with qualification. Rāzī's fellow theologians cite 39:62 and compare 30:27, taking the plural as what people believe. Asad reports al-Ṭabarī's secondary usage; al-Ṭabrisī and al-Ālūsī reserve origination from nothing for God. Al-Rāzī rejects inferring human origination from the word."}, {"id": "23:14/q22/p4", "position": "God's making surpasses statue-makers because He gives movement and spirit.", "reasons": "Muqātil compares inert statues; Yaḥyā cites image-makers who cannot breathe spirit and reports sayings warning that imitators must bring images to life or create even a fly, speck or mosquito. Al-Wāḥidī and Bursevī repeat the contrast."}, {"id": "23:14/q22/p5", "position": "The plural denotes actual human creators of their own acts.", "reasons": "The Muʿtazila argue that the comparative presupposes other creators and humans originate chosen acts by estimation; Al-Asʾila al-Muqḥima poses the same objection. Bursevī answers with image-makers who cannot breathe spirit (5:110), and al-Ālūsī reports the Muʿtazilite sense of independent production."}, {"id": "23:14/q22/p6", "position": "The superlative magnifies God's excellence without comparing Him with independent creators.", "reasons": "Islahi says Arabic afʿal with a plural can intensify rather than co

mpare; he rejects altering creator to a lesser sense and says God fashioned people in the best mould. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ proposes aḥsan from khaliq meaning worthy rather than a straightforward comparison from khalaqa; she reports al-Rāghib's God-without-model versus human-with-model distinction."}]}
{"id": "23:14/q23", "question": "What does 'best' say about God's creation and human evil acts?", "turns_on": "Whether goodness means flawless construction, moral goodness excluding evil acts, or the Creator's incomparable scope.", "positions": [{"id": "23:14/q23/p1", "position": "God's creating is unbounded, exact and free of defect.", "reasons": "Jishumī says God makes substances, accidents, life, death and agents without tools or limits; al-Ṭabrisī says His exact measure has no disparity; Elmalılı returns every created agency to Him."}, {"id": "23:14/q23/p2", "position": "Best means precise, well-composed creation; this does not exclude God's creation of unbelief and sin.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī answers the Muʿtazila that excellence can mean exact composition and that acts are good from God, who is subject to no higher command. Al-Ālūsī likewise says all is good insofar as it comes from God."}, {"id": "23:14/q23/p3", "position": "Because all God's creation is good and wise, He does not create unbelief or sin; humans originate those acts.", "reasons": "The Muʿtazila infer this from the praise and from their claim of deliberate human origination."}]}
{"id": "23:14/q24", "question": "Who first uttered the closing phrase in the reports?", "turns_on": "The named speaker and sequence vary, and the Ibn Abī Sarḥ and Muʿādh reports face chronological or transmission objections.", "positions": [{"id": "23:14/q24/p1", "position": "ʿUmar anticipated or concurred with the revealed ending.", "reasons": "Some reports have him speak as the Prophet paused, others after revelation began or before the matching ending descended; the Prophet is reported to say it was revealed that way. Al-Wāḥidī and al-Rāzī list it among four of ʿUmar's agreements, alongside the Station, veiling and admonition to wives. Al-Itqān treats Companion agreement as an occasion of revelation and reports a Prophetic saying that truth was put on ʿUmar's tongue and heart."}, {"id": "23:14/q24/p2", "position": "The scribe ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Sarḥ anticipated a phrase and then claimed prophethood or apostatized.", "reasons": "Accounts vary whether he anticipated the closing praise or 'another creation,' and whether he later converted at the conquest or died an unbeliever. Al-Ṭabrisī says, if sound, coincidence is possible and Ibn Abī Sarḥ was self-deceived; al-Nasafī objects that a Medinan apostasy conflicts with the Meccan sūra. Al-Ālūsī considers a Medinan verse or dictation, noting implications for al-Suyūṭī's Meccan exceptions."}, {"id": "23:14/q24/p3", "position": "Muʿādh ibn Jabal anticipated the ending.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Qurṭubī, al-Nasafī and Abū Ḥayyān report this variant. Zayd ibn Thābit's report has Muʿādh supply the words while the Prophet dictated, and the Prophet smile or laugh; Ibn Kathīr calls that report severely anomalous because the sūra is Meccan, but Zayd and Muʿādh belong to Medina."}, {"id": "23:14/q24/p4", "position": "The accounts may reflect memorable anticipations of an ending cued by its preceding words.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān's tawshīḥ or al-muṭmiʿ has an opening that makes its close foreseeable, like the supports of a sash; al-Ālūsī says strong Qurʾānic composition often reveals the ending. This helps explain coincident speech without treating it as revelation from the speaker."}]}
{"id": "23:14/q25", "question": "Does anticipation of the verse's words challenge its inimitability?", "turns_on": "Whether one predicted phrase is enough to rival the larger revealed discourse.", "positions": [{"id": "23:14/q25/p1", "position": "No: a coincident short phrase does not match the Qur'an's miraculous discourse.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says the utterance may fall below the amount where miraculous quality appears; Bursevī and al-Ālūsī compare the threshold of a complete shortest sūra. Al-Ṭabrisī says coincidence is possible and does not make the scribe a prophet. Al-Ālūsī says the ending depends on preceding composition."}, {"id": "23:14/q25/p2", "position": "The scribe's anticipation seemed to him to undermine the Prophet's claim.", "reasons": "In al-Rāzī's version Ibn Abī Sarḥ objects that a human had uttered comparable words; al-Rāzī rejects the inference."}]}
{"id": "23:14/q26", "question": "How is the closing praise used in Prophetic prayer?", "turns_on": "The reports agree on the praise in prostration; associated reports vary on prayer gestures.", "positions": [{"id": "23:14/q26/p1", "position": "The Prophet recited it in prostration while submitting to God and praising the creation of face, hearing and sight.", "reasons": "ʿAlī reports multiple forms in Musnad Aḥmad, Ibn Ḥibbān, Abū Dāwūd, Ibn Mājah, Muslim, al-Nasāʾī and al-Tirmidhī; al-Nasāʾī also transmits Jābir and Muḥammad b. Maslama, the latter in night prayer. Al-Tirmidhī grades the cited versions ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ."}, {"id": "23:14/q26/p2", "position": "A related prayer report includes hand raising at specified transitions, over which jurists differed.", "reasons": "Al-Tirmidhī reports al-Shāfiʿī and associates following the practice, Aḥmad not endorsing it, and some Kufans confining it to voluntary prayer; Sulaymān al-Hāshimī compares its transmission with al-Zuhrī's well-known chain."}]}
{"id": "23:14/q27", "question": "When does an embryo count as an infant for the withdrawal or infanticide discussion?", "turns_on": "The sources distinguish the completion of developmental stages from an earlier legally significant formed body.", "positions": [{"id": "23:14/q27/p1", "position": "Withdrawal is not minor infanticide before the embryo completes the seven stages.", "reasons": "ʿAlī's answer is reported by Ibn al-Jawzī and Ibn ʿĀshūr, with ʿUmar approving in the latter; Ibn ʿAbbās is also reported to reject calling withdrawal infanticide before those stages."}, {"id": "23:14/q27/p2", "position": "A formed embryo has legal effect for the carrying slave woman.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī says that once bones and flesh are formed it is a human child and its mother becomes an umm walad; al-Qurṭubī sends fuller legal discussion of the stages to his commentary on 22:5."}]}
{"id": "23:14/q28", "question": "What does the sequence show about God's power and resurrection?", "turns_on": "Whether the stages are used chiefly as proof of resurrection, divine lordship and design, or human honor and duty.", "positions": [{"id": "23:14/q28/p1", "position": "Creation from a tiny beginning through elaborate stages proves divine power, wisdom, mercy and ability to recreate the dead.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī says resurrection is easier than first making a human from nothing; Jishumī and al-Burhān frame the stages as an argument for the afterlife (75:40). {"id": "23:14/q33", "question": "What do related reports say about creation of Adam and the wider world?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:14/q33/p1", "position": "God diversifies bodies, senses and provision through His creative command.", "reasons": "Wahb's account of Adam adds clay, water, senses and a spirit for moral discernment and planning; the four-humor account links bodily balance to health. ʿUzayr describes heavens and earth separated from water, night and day, diverse animals from water (24:45), varied plants from one earth and water, and limbs and nourishment in the womb."}]}
{"id": "23:14/q34", "question": "What inward meaning is drawn from the creation and final praise?", "turns_on": "The inward readings range from divine names manifested in creation to personal spiritual realization.", "positions": [{"id": "23:14/q34/p1", "position": "The human is prepared for gnosis, love, servanthood and spiritual effacement.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī speaks of rare mature states and individual gifts of inspiration; al-Qāshānī interprets breathed divine spirit and image; Taʾwīlāt al-Najmiyya names the human a repository of gnosis and care. {"id": "23:14/q35", "question": "What linguistic or rhetorical parallels are cited around the verse?", "turns_on": "The notes use several literary, syntactic and lexical parallels to interpret the verse's conclusion and life theme.", "positions": [{"id": "23:14/q35/p1", "position": "The verse's ending is cued by its beginning, an example of tawshīḥ or al-muṭmiʿ.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān explains that the opening anticipates the end, comparing it with a sash; al-Itqān calls the conclusion apt and al-Ālūsī compares verses whose openings reveal their rhymes."}, {"id": "23:14/q35/p2", "position": "The broader lexicon of death contrasts life's creation with death or inert matter.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī distinguishes mawt, mawta, mawāt, madness-like usage and the place Muʾta; al-Dāmghānī calls semen dead before enlivening.
